routes.title: About · LearnDSA
routes.description: What LearnDSA is, who it's for, and how the interactive visualizations work.

routes.title: Renderer gallery (dev) · LearnDSA
routes.description: Dev-only renderer gallery.

routes.title: Glossary · LearnDSA
routes.description: A–Z reference of the data-structure and algorithm terms used across LearnDSA, each linked to the lesson that introduces it.

routes.title: LearnDSA — algorithms, Kubernetes and system design, one step at a time
routes.description: Free, interactive engineering courses. Step through algorithms on your own input, then learn the systems they run inside: Kubernetes from fundamentals to production, and system design from principles to real architectures.
h1: See how the machine actually works

headings.text: What an algorithms lesson actually does
Read the same run as a table
Run it on your own numbers
System Design: Principles and Real-World Architectures
Start where the rest of it builds from.

routes.title: Arrays · LearnDSA
routes.description: Contiguous, index-addressable storage: O(1) access, but O(n) insert and delete because elements must shift.

routes.title: Linear & Binary Search · LearnDSA
routes.description: Find an element in an array two ways: linear search scans every item in O(n); binary search halves a sorted range in O(log n).

routes.title: Complexity & Big-O · LearnDSA
routes.description: Measure how an algorithm's work grows with input size, and compare O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), and O(n²).

routes.title: Data Structures & Algorithms · LearnDSA
routes.description: Fifteen interactive lessons on the data structures and algorithms every engineer is expected to know. Each one is built around a visualization you can play, pause, step through and run on your own input.

routes.title: Intro to Dynamic Programming · LearnDSA
routes.description: Dynamic programming solves a problem by breaking it into overlapping subproblems, solving each once, and reusing the answers — turning exponential recursion into O(n) work.

routes.title: Graph Traversal: BFS & DFS · LearnDSA
routes.description: Two ways to visit every node of a graph — breadth-first search with a queue, and depth-first search with a stack — and how the choice of frontier changes the order.

routes.title: Graphs · LearnDSA
routes.description: Vertices joined by edges model networks; store them as an adjacency list or matrix, and choose which by trading space against edge-lookup speed.

routes.title: Hash Tables · LearnDSA
routes.description: Store keys by hashing them to buckets for near-instant lookup; handle collisions by chaining keys that land in the same bucket.

routes.title: Heaps · LearnDSA
routes.description: A binary heap is a complete tree kept in an array where every parent outranks its children, giving O(log n) insert and O(1) access to the max (or min).

routes.title: Learn · LearnDSA
routes.description: Every LearnDSA course: data structures and algorithms, Kubernetes, and system design — interactive lessons you work through at your own pace, free and without an account.

routes.title: Admission Control · LearnDSA
routes.description: The stage between authorization and storage where the cluster gets to have opinions of its own — mutating webhooks that rewrite an object, validating webhooks that refuse it, and the CEL policies that need no webhook at all.

routes.title: Selectors, Affinity and Anti-Affinity · LearnDSA
routes.description: Node labels give you a vocabulary for describing the kind of machine a Pod needs, and affinity turns that vocabulary into rules — some of them hard, some of them merely preferred, and some of them about the other Pods already there.

routes.title: Snapshots, Backup and Restore · LearnDSA
routes.description: VolumeSnapshots are fast, cheap and in the same failure domain as the volume they copy — which makes them a very good undo button and a very poor backup, and neither is worth anything until a restore has been rehearsed.

headings.text: Snapshots are a CSI feature delivered as ecosystem CRDs
A snapshot is crash-consistent, not application-consistent
Back up more than the bytes

routes.title: Bottlenecks and Capacity Planning · LearnDSA
routes.description: A cluster has no single capacity — it has several ceilings, and only the one you reach first has any effect on you, which is why capacity planning starts by finding out which one that is.

headings.text: Start with the node, not the cluster
Finding the number instead of assuming it

routes.title: ConfigMaps · LearnDSA
routes.description: A ConfigMap is a namespaced bag of string keys the cluster stores for you — enough to get settings out of the image, and deliberately far less than a configuration service.

routes.title: Cost Optimisation · LearnDSA
routes.description: A cluster bill is the capacity you reserved, not the capacity you used — so the money hides in the gap between requests and real usage, in node shapes that cannot be packed, and in the objects nothing ever deletes.

headings.text: The levers, and when not to pull them

routes.title: DaemonSets, Jobs and CronJobs · LearnDSA
routes.description: Three workloads where you do not choose the replica count: the node list chooses it, the amount of work chooses it, or the clock does.

routes.title: A Systematic Debugging Workflow · LearnDSA
routes.description: One order of commands for every broken workload — get, describe, events, logs, exec — because a Pod is built in that order and the first handover that failed is the only one worth reading.

headings.text: 1. kubectl get — where has it stopped?
2. kubectl describe — the object’s own account
5. kubectl exec — asking the running process
Reaching a Pod without the Service path

routes.title: Deployments and ReplicaSets · LearnDSA
routes.description: A Deployment is version control for a Pod template: each distinct template gets a ReplicaSet, and a rollout is the Deployment moving replicas from one of them to another while you watch.

routes.title: Desired State and Reconciliation · LearnDSA
routes.description: A controller reads the whole object rather than the event that woke it — which is why it recovers from a dropped message, a restart, and a situation nobody designed for.

routes.title: PodDisruptionBudgets · LearnDSA
routes.description: A PodDisruptionBudget is a veto held by the eviction API: it makes a request to remove a Pod fail, which protects you from a node drain and does nothing whatsoever about a node that dies.

routes.title: DNS and Service Discovery · LearnDSA
routes.description: Cluster DNS turns a Service name into an address and stops there; the dataplane turns that address into a Pod. Most "DNS problems" are one half working perfectly while the other half has nothing to deliver to.

routes.title: etcd, HA and Disaster Recovery · LearnDSA
routes.description: Every part of a cluster can be rebuilt from an image except the one datastore that holds what you asked for — which makes etcd the only thing worth a real backup, and a restore nobody has rehearsed worth very little.

headings.text: What is in etcd, and what is not
What a control-plane outage actually stops

routes.title: Event-Driven Scaling · LearnDSA
routes.description: A worker blocked on the network looks idle to a CPU metric, so the signal that actually tracks its load is the backlog waiting for it — which is what event-driven autoscaling reads, down to and including zero replicas.

headings.text: Getting the number into the cluster

routes.title: GitOps and Environment Management · LearnDSA
routes.description: GitOps moves the reconciliation boundary one step out: the repository holds the desired state and an agent inside the cluster closes the gap, which turns a deploy into a merge and drift into something that corrects itself.

routes.title: Graceful Shutdown · LearnDSA
routes.description: Deleting a Pod starts two clocks that nobody synchronises — the routing update spreading across the cluster, and the kubelet counting down to SIGKILL — and the gap between them is where dropped requests come from.

routes.title: Helm · LearnDSA
routes.description: Helm is a text templating engine with a release ledger: it renders manifests on your machine and remembers the exact set it sent, which is what makes an upgrade a diff and a rollback a restore.

headings.text: A release is what the cluster remembers
Reading a chart you did not write

routes.title: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler · LearnDSA
routes.description: An HPA is not a rule engine that adds a Pod above eighty percent — it divides measured load by your target, multiplies the replica count by that ratio, and moves there in one step.

headings.text: The signal, and where the number comes from
What it does with the number

routes.title: How Scheduling Works · LearnDSA
routes.description: The scheduler filters every node down to the ones a Pod could run on, scores the survivors, writes one name into the Pod — and then never thinks about that Pod again.

routes.title: Image Security and the Supply Chain · LearnDSA
routes.description: A scanner proves a known vulnerability is present, a signature proves who published the bytes, and an SBOM is an inventory — three different claims, none of which is the claim that an image is safe.
h1: Image Security and the Supply Chain

routes.title: Immutable Images and Tagging · LearnDSA
routes.description: A Deployment compares Pod templates, not registries, so a tag that can move turns a release into a change nothing recorded and a rollback into a no-op that reports success.

routes.title: Ingress and the Gateway API · LearnDSA
routes.description: One front door, many hostnames and paths: Ingress made HTTP routing a Kubernetes object, and the Gateway API is the project answer to everything Ingress could only express in vendor annotations.

routes.title: Init Containers and Sidecars · LearnDSA
routes.description: Init containers run in order and finish; a native sidecar is an init container that starts in order and keeps running — which is what finally made a proxy safe to put in a Job.

routes.title: Injecting Configuration · LearnDSA
routes.description: Environment variables are read once when a process starts and mounted files are updated in place — which is why the injection you choose decides what happens the next time the configuration changes.

routes.title: Kustomize · LearnDSA
routes.description: Kustomize expresses the difference between two environments as a patch on real manifests, so every input and every output is a document you can read — and there is deliberately no way to write a conditional.

routes.title: Labels, Selectors and Annotations · LearnDSA
routes.description: Nothing in Kubernetes holds a reference to a Pod. A Service, a ReplicaSet and a NetworkPolicy each find their Pods by running a query, which is what makes a label an interface rather than a note to yourself.

routes.title: A Local Cluster for the Exercises · LearnDSA
routes.description: Ten minutes to a real API server on your own machine with kind, minikube or k3d — plus an honest list of what none of them reproduce.
h1: A Local Cluster for the Exercises

routes.title: Logs and Events · LearnDSA
routes.description: A log is your application talking about itself; an event is the cluster talking about your object — two different records, both stored badly on purpose, and both gone sooner than you expect.

routes.title: Metrics · LearnDSA
routes.description: Three different things are called metrics in a cluster — resource usage, object state and application counters — and a Prometheus-style server pulls all of them into one time series database you can ask questions of.

routes.title: Monitoring Architecture and Alerting · LearnDSA
routes.description: Assemble logs, metrics and traces into one pipeline, then page on the handful of symptoms a user can feel — because an alert nobody can act on trains people to ignore the ones they can.

headings.text: Alerting on a budget rather than a threshold

routes.title: Multi-Environment Strategy · LearnDSA
routes.description: A namespace divides one cluster into scopes for names, budgets and permissions; a separate cluster divides the control plane itself — so choosing between them is choosing a blast radius, and the safer answer is paid for at every upgrade.

headings.text: The part that is not topology

routes.title: Multi-Tenancy · LearnDSA
routes.description: A namespace gives a tenant names of its own; every other part of a boundary — permissions, budget, network, workload rules, nodes — is assembled on top of it, and a short list of things tenants share cannot be divided at any price.

headings.text: When a separate cluster is the honest answer
Posture is what is true by default

routes.title: Namespaces and kubectl Essentials · LearnDSA
routes.description: A namespace is a scope for names, not a wall between tenants — and every kubectl command you will ever type is a verb, a kind, a name, a namespace and a context.

routes.title: DNS and Service Connectivity · LearnDSA
routes.description: One request from a Pod to a Service crosses four systems that fail separately — the name, the address, the endpoint list and the listening process — and each hop has a command that proves it.

headings.text: 2. Does the ClusterIP accept a connection?
4. Is the process listening, and where?

routes.title: NetworkPolicies · LearnDSA
routes.description: Selecting a Pod with any NetworkPolicy flips that Pod to default-deny for that direction — and the object is accepted and stored whether or not your CNI plugin enforces a single rule of it.

routes.title: The Networking Model · LearnDSA
routes.description: Kubernetes ships no networking implementation at all — it states three rules any implementation must satisfy, and every Service, DNS name and NetworkPolicy you will meet is built on top of them.

routes.title: Objects, Manifests and the API · LearnDSA
routes.description: Every Kubernetes object has the same four top-level fields, so once you can read those, a kind you have never met is still a manifest you can write.

routes.title: CRDs and Operators · LearnDSA
routes.description: A CustomResourceDefinition adds a noun to the Kubernetes API and a controller adds the verb, which together turn a runbook into a control loop — at the cost of one more controller that you now own and upgrade.

routes.title: PersistentVolumes and Claims · LearnDSA
routes.description: A claim is what an application asks for and a PersistentVolume is what the cluster supplies — a split that keeps disk identifiers out of your manifests, and puts the reclaim policy in charge of whether your data survives.

headings.text: Phases, and what they are telling you
The reclaim policy decides whether the data survives

routes.title: Pod Security Admission · LearnDSA
routes.description: Three Pod Security Standards, three modes, and a pair of namespace labels — a built-in admission controller that rejects a Pod at creation and never touches the ones already running.

headings.text: The surprise: it checks Pods, not Deployments
Rolling it out to a live namespace

routes.title: CrashLoopBackOff and ImagePullBackOff · LearnDSA
routes.description: Both names describe a timer the kubelet is running, not a fault — the cause is in the event that precedes the back-off, or in the container’s last exit code.

headings.text: ImagePullBackOff: the kubelet cannot get the image
CrashLoopBackOff: the container starts and stops

routes.title: Pods and the Pod Lifecycle · LearnDSA
routes.description: A Pod is one small shared machine — a single address, a single set of volumes, a single scheduling decision — and it moves through five phases that the status column deliberately does not show you.

routes.title: Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes · LearnDSA
routes.description: Three probes answer three different questions — send traffic here, restart this container, and has it finished booting — and the most damaging mistake in Kubernetes is answering the second one with a check on somebody else.

routes.title: Project: Configuration, Secrets and Storage · LearnDSA
routes.description: Give the project settings, credentials and a disk — and meet the moment a volume stops three interchangeable replicas from being interchangeable.

headings.text: Making a change reach the container

routes.title: Project: Health, Autoscaling and a Safe Rollout · LearnDSA
routes.description: Teach the project to report its own health, size itself against load, and refuse to finish a rollout that would take the working version away.
h1: Project: Health, Autoscaling and a Safe Rollout

headings.text: Requests, because the autoscaler measures against them

routes.title: Project: Observe and Troubleshoot It · LearnDSA
routes.description: Learn what the project looks like when it is healthy, then break it three ways on purpose and find each fault by walking the workflow instead of guessing.

headings.text: Fault 1: a tag that does not exist
Fault 2: a selector that matches nothing
Fault 3: a reference that stops resolving

routes.title: Project: A Stateless Web Service · LearnDSA
routes.description: Build the running project the rest of this module extends: two Deployments in their own namespace, each behind a Service, with one calling the other by name.

routes.title: Quotas, Limits, Priority and Preemption · LearnDSA
routes.description: A ResourceQuota caps what a namespace may ask for and a LimitRange fills in what its authors forgot, while PriorityClasses decide whose Pod gets the last free space — and whose Pod is removed to make it.

routes.title: RBAC and ServiceAccounts · LearnDSA
routes.description: RBAC is a permit book with no eraser: a binding grants, nothing revokes, and the only honest way to know what a subject can do is to ask the API server with kubectl auth can-i.

routes.title: Requests, Limits and QoS · LearnDSA
routes.description: A request is a booking the scheduler does arithmetic with; a limit is a fuse the kubelet wires into the container — and the pair of them decides which quality-of-service class you land in when the node runs short.

routes.title: Rolling Updates and Rollback · LearnDSA
routes.description: A rollout is a state machine you can watch, pause and reverse — and the history it keeps is a stack of Pod templates, which is both what makes rollback instant and what makes it incomplete.

routes.title: Readiness and Broken Rollouts · LearnDSA
routes.description: A rollout that will not finish is a controller refusing to break its own availability budget — the old version is still serving, nothing rolls back by itself, and one table tells you which.

headings.text: One table says which situation you are in
Which of four families is it?

routes.title: Blue/Green and Canary · LearnDSA
routes.description: A rolling update spreads the risk of a release across every user; blue/green and canary decide instead who is exposed, for how long, and how fast you can take it back.

headings.text: Canary: a small share, on purpose

routes.title: Pending Pods · LearnDSA
routes.description: A Pending Pod is one nobody has been told to run — and one field, plus one event, separates insufficient capacity from a taint, a label, a volume and a quota that stopped the Pod ever being created.

headings.text: Step one: does it have a node?
Step two: read the whole scheduling message
When more nodes are the answer, and when they are not

routes.title: Secret Management in Practice · LearnDSA
routes.description: Who can read this credential today, and how do you shorten that list — encryption at rest, external stores, and a rotation that ends with the old value revoked.

routes.title: Secrets · LearnDSA
routes.description: A Secret is a ConfigMap with a different name, a separate RBAC surface and better manners — and base64 is an encoding, so out of the box the value sits in etcd in the clear.

routes.title: Security Contexts · LearnDSA
routes.description: The fields that decide what a container may do to the node it lands on: which user it runs as, which capabilities it keeps, and whether it can write to its own filesystem.

routes.title: Services · LearnDSA
routes.description: A Service is a stable address in front of a changing set of Pods — and ClusterIP, NodePort and LoadBalancer are not three mechanisms but one, with progressively more of the outside world attached.

routes.title: StatefulSets with Persistent Data · LearnDSA
routes.description: A volumeClaimTemplate stamps out one claim per replica and names it after the ordinal, which is what lets a replica come back to its own data — and what leaves a row of disks behind every time you scale down.

routes.title: StatefulSets · LearnDSA
routes.description: A StatefulSet trades interchangeability for identity: stable names, stable DNS and one volume per replica — none of which makes your application clustered, and all of which makes every rollout slower.

routes.title: StorageClasses and Access Modes · LearnDSA
routes.description: A StorageClass turns a claim into a real disk without anyone pre-creating one, and an access mode is a property the backing storage either has or does not — ReadWriteMany least of all.

headings.text: Access modes are a property of the volume, not a wish

routes.title: Taints, Tolerations and Topology Spread · LearnDSA
routes.description: A taint lets a node refuse Pods that have not been given permission to be there, and a topology spread constraint turns "keep my replicas apart" from an all-or-nothing rule into a dial you can set.

routes.title: Traces · LearnDSA
routes.description: A trace is the itinerary of one request across every service that touched it — spans, a shared trace id, and a header that has to survive every hop or the picture breaks in half.

routes.title: Cluster Upgrades and Version Skew · LearnDSA
routes.description: Kubernetes supports a documented window in which its components may disagree about their version, and an upgrade is the exercise of moving through that window in the right order — control plane first, one minor at a time, one node at a time.

routes.title: Vertical and Cluster Autoscaling · LearnDSA
routes.description: A VerticalPodAutoscaler changes how big a Pod asks to be, and a cluster autoscaler changes how many machines there are to put it on — both of them reading requests rather than usage.

headings.text: Vertical: making the request match reality

routes.title: Ephemeral Storage and Volumes · LearnDSA
routes.description: A container writes into a thin layer that is destroyed the moment the container is replaced; a volume is a directory the Pod owns, and picking the right lifetime is most of what storage asks of you.

headings.text: Ephemeral storage is a scheduled resource

routes.title: What Kubernetes Is · LearnDSA
routes.description: Kubernetes is a set of control loops over a declarative API: you write down the state you want, and controllers spend the rest of the cluster’s life making reality match it.

routes.title: Kubernetes: From Fundamentals to Production · LearnDSA
routes.description: A complete path from "what is an orchestrator" to running, securing, scaling and debugging real workloads. Written for Kubernetes 1.36, using only current APIs, with a working manifest or command in every lesson.

headings.text: A Local Cluster for the Exercises
Image Security and the Supply Chain
Project: Health, Autoscaling and a Safe Rollout

routes.title: Linked Lists · LearnDSA
routes.description: Nodes joined by pointers: O(1) insert and delete at a known spot, but O(n) to reach a position because there is no random access.

routes.title: Queues · LearnDSA
routes.description: A FIFO collection: enqueue at the rear, dequeue at the front, both O(1). A circular buffer reuses freed slots by wrapping around.

routes.title: Recursion · LearnDSA
routes.description: A function that calls itself, breaking a problem into a smaller version of itself until it reaches a base case — with the call stack keeping track.

routes.title: API Design and Data Modelling · LearnDSA
routes.description: The contract outlives the implementation, which is why the API comes before the schema. Entities, idempotent writes, pagination that survives inserts, and versioning you can afford.

routes.title: Availability and Durability · LearnDSA
routes.description: Nines are an error budget, not a slogan: what they cost per month, how dependencies multiply them down, and why durability is a separate promise that replication alone does not keep.

routes.title: Caching · LearnDSA
routes.description: A cache is not a decision until it names a key, a TTL and an invalidation event. Placement, cache-aside, stampedes, cold starts — and the arithmetic showing when the cache became load-bearing.

routes.title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation · LearnDSA
routes.description: A five-step method that turns stated assumptions into QPS, storage and bandwidth, plus the table of reference numbers to estimate against.

routes.title: Content Delivery Networks · LearnDSA
routes.description: A CDN is a fleet of caching reverse proxies near your readers. What it buys — distance and origin offload — plus cache keys, Vary, what must never be cached, and the fetch storm you cause yourself.

routes.title: Applying It to a New Problem · LearnDSA
routes.description: Place, predict, price, check — a four-step method that turns an unfamiliar product into a set of dial positions and a predicted architecture, worked through a live game-streaming platform.
h1: Applying It to a New Problem

routes.title: Three Platforms Side by Side · LearnDSA
routes.description: Eleven concerns across a streaming, a music and a video-sharing platform, read down each column as one shape and across each row as one spectrum — with the audiences normalised so the comparison is about design rather than about assumptions.

routes.title: Why the Architectures Differ · LearnDSA
routes.description: Four dials — item shape, catalogue shape, popularity shape and write shape — plus trust and a latency floor, and the chain from each one to the mechanism it forces.

routes.title: Consistency Models, CAP and PACELC · LearnDSA
routes.description: A consistency model is the contract about what a read may return. Strong, eventual and the session guarantees between them — what a partition forces, and what PACELC says about the other 99.9% of the time.

routes.title: A Repeatable Design Workflow · LearnDSA
routes.description: Thirteen steps that turn "design a system like X" from a blank page into a sequence of small, answerable questions — and the rule that every answer names its trade-off.

routes.title: Event Streams · LearnDSA
routes.description: A log retains records and hands every reader its own offset, so consumers are independent and the past can be replayed — the opposite of a queue in almost every property that matters.

routes.title: Idempotency, Retries and Backpressure · LearnDSA
routes.description: A timeout tells you nothing about whether the work happened. Idempotency keys, backoff with jitter, circuit breakers and bounded queues — and the retry storm you generate yourself.

routes.title: Latency and Throughput · LearnDSA
routes.description: Latency is a distribution and throughput is a rate. Percentiles, queueing and the arithmetic tying the two together — and why p99, not the average, is the number a design is judged on.

routes.title: Load Balancers and Reverse Proxies · LearnDSA
routes.description: A load balancer is one job a reverse proxy does. What L4 and L7 can each see, how health checking decides who receives traffic, and the work a proxy does that has nothing to do with spreading load.

routes.title: Message Queues · LearnDSA
routes.description: A queue hands each unit of work to whichever consumer is free, deletes it on acknowledgement and redelivers it when nobody answers — which is what makes at-least-once the honest default and a dead-letter queue an ongoing commitment.

routes.title: High-Level Architecture · LearnDSA
routes.description: The boxes of a Netflix-like platform — edge, gateway, catalogue, discovery, playback, viewing state, event pipeline — and what breaks if you take each one away.

routes.title: Watch History and Continue Watching · LearnDSA
routes.description: One mutable cursor per profile and title, one append-only log behind it, a write rate generated by streams rather than by taps — and the consistency guarantee that actually matters when you pause on a television and open a phone.

routes.title: Personalisation and Experimentation · LearnDSA
routes.description: Ranking a catalogue of tens of thousands per profile — offline, nearline and online — and running the experiments that decide whether a ranking change was an improvement at all.

routes.title: Scale, Reliability and Degradation · LearnDSA
routes.description: What a cache hit ratio is worth in origin capacity at 90 Tbps, how a region is evacuated, the order in which the product sheds features, and the conditions that make failure injection responsible rather than reckless.

routes.title: Requirements and Scale · LearnDSA
routes.description: What a Netflix-like platform has to do — accounts, profiles, catalogue, playback on many devices — and the estimate that turns those features into tens of terabits per second over a catalogue of only a few petabytes.

routes.title: Video Delivery · LearnDSA
routes.description: Encode once, cut into segments, let the client pick a rendition per segment, and cache the bytes near viewers — plus the two numbers that explain why no application server is ever on the byte path.

routes.title: NoSQL Databases · LearnDSA
routes.description: Four families — key-value, document, wide-column and graph — each giving up a different relational guarantee to buy a different property, and how to pick one from your access patterns instead of from the label.

routes.title: Object Storage · LearnDSA
routes.description: A durable key-to-blob store reachable over HTTP — where images, video and backups belong, why a database row should hold a key rather than the bytes, and the four filesystem habits it does not support.

routes.title: Observability, Failure Handling and DR · LearnDSA
routes.description: Metrics, logs and traces answer three different questions at three different costs; degradation is what you designed before the incident; and RPO and RTO are two separate promises that a restore you have never run keeps neither of.

routes.title: Rate Limiting · LearnDSA
routes.description: Fixed window, sliding window and token bucket, with the arithmetic for each — and why enforcing one limit across a fleet is a distributed-counter problem rather than a configuration setting.

routes.title: Relational Databases · LearnDSA
routes.description: What a transaction and an isolation level actually promise, what a composite index costs on every write, and the specific places a single relational primary bends — which is not the same as "SQL does not scale".

routes.title: Replication, Partitioning and Sharding · LearnDSA
routes.description: Replication copies the same data and buys reads and durability; sharding splits different data and buys writes. Why they are not interchangeable, and why the shard key is the decision you cannot undo cheaply.

routes.title: Functional and Non-Functional Requirements · LearnDSA
routes.description: Turn a vague brief into a list of what the system does, a shorter list of numbers saying how well it must do it, and an out-of-scope list that keeps the design finishable.

routes.title: Search Indexes · LearnDSA
routes.description: An inverted index turns "what is in this document?" into "which documents contain this term?" — plus ranking, the freshness lag that comes with a second copy of your data, and why search is its own system.

routes.title: Service Discovery and Coordination · LearnDSA
routes.description: Discovery is a naming problem solved with a registry that is always slightly stale; coordination is an agreement problem solved with consensus, which costs a majority round trip per decision and still needs fencing tokens.

routes.title: Architecture and the Two Paths · LearnDSA
routes.description: Catalogue, playlist, playback and event services drawn around the stores they own — plus the one line that decides which side of the platform a piece of work belongs on.

routes.title: Audio Delivery and Offline · LearnDSA
routes.description: Immutable three-megabyte files, a rendition ladder, prefetch and client caches — and why rights are enforced when a URL is signed rather than when a byte is cached.

routes.title: Playlist Consistency · LearnDSA
routes.description: A playlist is a sequence of operations, not a document — which is what lets two phones and a collaborator edit it at once without anybody losing a track.

routes.title: The Recommendation Pipeline · LearnDSA
routes.description: Events to features to candidates to ranking to feedback: the two-stage funnel that turns a hundred million tracks into thirty, and which half of it runs offline.

routes.title: Scale, Events and Reliability · LearnDSA
routes.description: Fifty thousand listening events a second with four consumers that need different guarantees, the bursts that arrive on a schedule, and a degradation ladder written before the outage.

routes.title: Requirements and Request Rate · LearnDSA
routes.description: A hundred million tracks, sessions that touch dozens of them, and the estimate that shows why request rate rather than bandwidth is the number this design has to answer.

routes.title: Reasoning About Trade-offs · LearnDSA
routes.description: A decision is a choice, a reason and an accepted cost. Write all three, name the alternative you rejected, and say what would make you revisit it.

routes.title: Workers and Schedulers · LearnDSA
routes.description: Workers run the work the request path handed off; schedulers decide when work appears with no request behind it. Leases, overlap, missed fires, and why a triggered job still has to be idempotent.

routes.title: Comments, Counters and Notifications · LearnDSA
routes.description: The real write firehose is views, not comments — counters as an aggregated stream, threads that paginate on a cursor and are moderated at write time, and notification fan-out that changes shape above a subscriber cutoff.

routes.title: Playback and Delivery · LearnDSA
routes.description: The same manifests and segments as any streaming platform, filled the opposite way: pull-through caching over an unpredictable catalogue, a tiered hierarchy that absorbs the tail, and what a video going viral does to a cold cache.

routes.title: Recommendations · LearnDSA
routes.description: Candidate generation and ranking as the 2016 RecSys paper describes them, the arithmetic that makes two stages compulsory over a billion videos, and what a mostly-cold corpus and a closed feedback loop do to both.

routes.title: Requirements and an Unbounded Catalogue · LearnDSA
routes.description: What a YouTube-like platform has to do when anyone may upload — and the estimate that turns a billion videos and a long tail into terabits per second of egress, petabytes a day of new storage, and a transcoding fleet.

routes.title: Storage, Bandwidth and Failure · LearnDSA
routes.description: Three cost centres with three different shapes, the levers that actually move each one, and a subsystem-by-subsystem account of what a lost region does to uploads, transcoding, counters and playback.

routes.title: Search · LearnDSA
routes.description: Searching a billion videos is searching the text around them: a document-partitioned inverted index, a second index that carries the last few hours, ranking that spam fights back against, and autocomplete built from the query log.

routes.title: Upload and Transcoding · LearnDSA
routes.description: A resumable upload that ends at object storage, an event that starts everything else, and the queue-and-worker pipeline that transcodes, thumbnails, checks and finally publishes a video.

routes.title: Sorting I: Bubble, Selection, Insertion · LearnDSA
routes.description: Three simple comparison sorts — bubble, selection, and insertion — that reorder an array in place by comparing and swapping, and why they all run in O(n²).

routes.title: Sorting II: Merge & Quick · LearnDSA
routes.description: Two divide-and-conquer sorts — merge sort and quick sort — that break the array in half, sort the pieces, and combine them to reach O(n log n).

routes.title: Stacks · LearnDSA
routes.description: A LIFO collection: push and pop happen at one end, the top, and both are O(1).

routes.title: System Design: Principles and Real-World Architectures · LearnDSA
routes.description: A repeatable design workflow, the distributed-systems building blocks it draws on, and three applied case studies: a Netflix-like, a Spotify-like and a YouTube-like platform, ending in a comparison of why similar products need different architectures.
h1: System Design: Principles and Real-World Architectures

headings.text: Applying It to a New Problem

routes.title: Trees & Binary Search Trees · LearnDSA
routes.description: A binary search tree keeps values ordered — smaller on the left, larger on the right — so insert and search follow one path down and run in O(log n) when balanced.
